input: What muscles does a deadlift work?
reference_facts: primary: glutes, hamstrings, erectors / lower back
secondary: lats, traps, forearms, quads
hip-hinge dominant movement pattern

input: What's the difference between a back squat and a front squat?
reference_facts: bar position: back of shoulders vs front rack
front squat shifts emphasis toward quads and demands more upright torso
back squat allows heavier loads, more posterior-chain involvement

input: Which joints does a Romanian deadlift load?
reference_facts: hip joint is the primary mover (hinge)
knee remains relatively static (soft bend)
lumbar spine loaded isometrically as bracer
gradually increasing demand over time
can be load, volume, density, range of motion, or technical complexity
required for continued adaptation

input: What does eccentric vs concentric mean?
reference_facts: concentric = muscle shortens under load (lifting phase)
eccentric = muscle lengthens under load (lowering phase)
eccentrics typically allow more load and cause more muscle damage

input: Why do glutes matter for athletes?
reference_facts: largest muscle group in the body
primary hip extensor — drives sprinting, jumping, change of direction
stabilizes the pelvis

input: How does training frequency affect hypertrophy?
reference_facts: higher frequency per muscle group generally improves hypertrophy up to a point
volume per session matters too — too high frequency with low volume per session may underperform
research suggests 2x per week per muscle group as a reasonable baseline

input: Talk to me about anti-rotation core work
reference_facts: anti-rotation trains the core to resist twisting forces
examples include Pallof press, suitcase carries, dead bug variations
more functionally relevant than isolated trunk rotation for most athletes

input: What's the role of the lats in a pull-up?
reference_facts: primary mover for shoulder adduction and extension
responsible for pulling the elbow toward the hip
biceps assist but lats do most of the work

input: Define unilateral training and why it matters
reference_facts: training one side at a time (split squats, single-arm rows)
addresses side-to-side strength imbalances
challenges core stability and proprioception more than bilateral work
